summary: Specifies a DHCP option, for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, that carries civic location such as country, state, city and street address. It can describe the location of the client or of the DHCP server.

eli5.summary: When a device joins a network, it can be told its street address. This note adds a spot in the setup message for country, city and street, so emergency services can find you.

questions: what is a catype in dhcp
subtitle: A DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option that hands a device its street address: country, state, city, street, building and more.

tldr.problem: Devices such as IP phones need to know where they are, to reach the right emergency response agency and to be found by responders. Civic addresses (street addresses) are easier to get than coordinates for most buildings, but address formats differ from country to country.
tldr.mechanism: A DHCP option carries a country code, a 'what' value saying whose location it is, and a list of type-length-value address elements. Elements can repeat in several languages and scripts.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4676, which had the wrong DHCPv6 option code. RFC 5774 and RFC 6848 later updated it.

today: RFC 4776 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4676 (RFC 4676), which had the wrong numeric value for the DHCPv6 option code. It has been updated by RFC 5774 and RFC 6848.

sections.title: Why Devices Need a Civic Address
sections.content:
Many services benefit from knowing roughly where a device is. IP telephony devices in particular need their location to contact the right emergency response agency and to be found by responders. Location comes in two forms: geospatial coordinates (longitude, latitude, altitude) and civic addresses (a street address). A related document, RFC 3825, covers coordinates for DHCPv4. Both can be used at once.

Civic addresses are useful because they give human-usable detail inside buildings and are readily available for most occupied structures. The RFC only defines delivery from the DHCP server to the client, not the other direction, for security reasons. It does not set criteria for when to give the location of the server or a nearby network element, and says DHCP configuration SHOULD NOT be used for emergency services without guidelines on the considerations involved.

If a network gives civic information over both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, the two MUST agree. Servers SHOULD return the option only when the client asked for it in its parameter request list (DHCPv4) or OPTION_ORO (DHCPv6).
sections.eli5: If you call for help from a phone you cannot see out of, someone needs to know which building you are in. The network can tell the phone its address when it connects.

sections.title: The Option in DHCPv4 and DHCPv6
sections.content:
In DHCPv4 the option code is 99 (GEOCONF_CIVIC). It has a length N of at least 3 octets, a what byte, a two-letter country code and then civic address elements. If the option is longer than the DHCPv4 maximum of 255 octets, the long-options mechanism of RFC 3396 MUST be used.

In DHCPv6 the option is OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC, code 36, with an option-len field, then the same what, country code and elements. The DHCPv6 option refers to the client as a whole.

The what value says whose location it is: 0 for the DHCP server, 1 for the network element believed closest to the client, and 2 for the client. Value 2 SHOULD be used, though it may not be known. Values 0 and 1 SHOULD NOT be used unless the client is known to be physically close. The country code is the two-letter ISO 3166 code in capital ASCII letters, such as DE or US.
sections.eli5: The message starts with a label saying whose address this is (the server's, a nearby box's, or yours) and the country, then lists the address pieces.

sections.title: Address Elements, Languages and Scripts
sections.content:
Each civic address element is a one-octet CAtype, a one-octet CAlength (the length of the value, not counting the length field) and a CAvalue. All elements are optional and can appear in any order. Values MUST be encoded as UTF-8 and SHOULD be written in mixed case. Abbreviations MUST NOT be used unless the element says so.

The same address can be written in several languages and scripts, for example Korean addresses in Hangul, Latin and Kanji. DHCP cannot ask for a particular language, so the server SHOULD send all common renderings and MUST send at least the one for the local language and script. It repeats the address elements, each run starting with a language element (CAtype 0) and/or a script element (CAtype 128). Those stay in effect until replaced. The defaults are i-default for language and Latn for script.

It is RECOMMENDED to group elements by script and language, and elements SHOULD appear in increasing CAtype order. The client collects elements by CAtype and picks the rendition it prefers.
sections.eli5: Each piece of the address is a little labeled box. If the address is written in more than one language, you get one set of boxes per language.

sections.title: Civic Address Components
sections.content:
Countries divide land differently, so the RFC uses five generic levels above street level: A1 (state, canton, region, province, prefecture), A2 (county, parish and similar), A3 (city or township), A4 (city division, borough, ward) and A5 (neighborhood, block). A6 is a group of streets below the neighborhood level. For Canada, Germany, Japan, Korea and the United States the RFC says how these map to local divisions. For example, in the US A1 is the state, using the two-letter abbreviations from the US Postal Service, and A3 is the civic community name.

More element types cover the street and the place itself: leading street direction, trailing street suffix, street suffix or type, house number and its suffix, landmark, additional location information, name of the occupant, postal code, building, unit, floor, room, type of place, postal community name, post office box, additional code, seat, and road elements (primary road, road section, branch road, sub-branch road, street name pre- and post-modifiers). Many of these correspond to US National Emergency Number Association (NENA) data names and to elements of the presence-based location object format in RFC 4119.
sections.eli5: An address is like nesting dolls: country, then state, then city, then street, then building, then room. Each piece gets its own number so the receiver knows which is which.

sections.title: Building a Postal Address
sections.content:
A recipient can build a postal address from the language-appropriate elements, including the postal code (CAtype 24). Two elements override civic ones. A post office box (CAtype 31) replaces the street address components (CAtype 34, PRD, POD, STS, HNO, HNS). A postal community name (CAtype 30) replaces the civic community name, typically A3.

Making a valid postal address takes country-specific knowledge, and the formatting of such addresses is outside this document. Post office boxes alone would be unsuitable as a location for emergency purposes.
sections.eli5: The same place can have a mail address and a street address. If there is a mailbox number, the mail address uses that instead of the street.

sections.title: Example: Munich City Hall
sections.content: The RFC shows a symbolic example (not the byte layout) for the Munich city hall in Bavaria, Germany. The first run is in German (de, script Latn) and gives the state, county, city, street, house number 8, landmark Rathaus, postal code 80331, type of place government-building and a post office box. Two more runs repeat the state and city in English (en) and Italian (it). Items that are the same in every language are given once.
sections.eli5: Munich city hall's address is written once in German, then the changing words (state and city name) again in English and Italian, so each reader sees a familiar spelling.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of the GEOPRIV architecture (RFC 3693) apply. The mechanism here is what that architecture calls a sighting function, which is not required to have security capabilities and is meant only for trusted, controlled environments. Where critical decisions rely on the option, DHCPv4 authentication from RFC 3118 SHOULD be used to protect its integrity.

DHCP messages have no privacy protection, so an eavesdropper on the link between server and client can read the location. Using the option on networks without access restrictions or network-layer or link-layer privacy is NOT RECOMMENDED. To limit exposure, servers SHOULD return it only when the client asked for it. Location information SHOULD NOT be sent from a DHCP client to a server, because doing so implicitly grants the server unlimited retention and distribution permissions.
sections.eli5: Anyone listening on the network could read the address, so only use this on networks where that is safe, and only hand it to devices that ask.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA registered new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option codes for the civic address option. The RFC also creates a registry for CAtypes, run under both Expert Review and Specification Required rules, with an Expert Reviewer appointed by the IESG. Each registration has a numeric CAtype assigned by IANA, a brief description, a reference to a published specification, and country-specific notes where relevant. The initial entries are the ones listed in the RFC's section 3.4. Country notes themselves are descriptive, not registrations, and may be written up in documents titled for the country.
sections.eli5: A shared list keeps track of which number means which kind of address piece, and new ones can be added after an expert says yes.

fields.name: what
fields.desc: Whose location this is: server (0), nearby network element (1) or client (2).

fields.name: country code
fields.desc: Two-letter ISO 3166 code in capital ASCII letters.

items.label: DHCP server
items.desc: Location of the DHCP server; SHOULD NOT be used unless the client is physically close.

items.label: Network element
items.desc: Location of the element believed closest to the client; same caution.

items.label: Client
items.desc: Location of the client. SHOULD be used, but may not be known.

items.label: language
items.desc: Language of the elements that follow; default i-default.

items.label: A1
items.desc: National subdivisions (state, canton, region, province, prefecture).

items.label: A4
items.desc: City division, borough, city district, ward, chou (JP).

items.label: A6
items.desc: Group of streets below the neighborhood level.

items.label: primary road name
items.desc: Road or street name associated with the address.

items.label: script
items.desc: Script of the elements that follow; default Latn.
